items.definition: Cloud infrastructure used by one organisation only, hosted on-site or at a dedicated facility.
items.examples: A hospital storing patient records; a bank's own cloud for financial data.
items.examTip: More control and security, but higher cost than public cloud.
keyFacts: Full control over data and security, so the organisation sets its own access rules and can meet GDPR for sensitive records
Higher set-up and running costs, because it must buy, house and maintain its own servers and pay staff to run them
Suits sensitive data (medical, financial), as nothing sits on hardware shared with other customers
Not shared with other organisations, so performance is predictable and never slowed by someone else's demand

items.definition: Cloud services shared by many organisations, run by a provider such as AWS or Azure.
items.examples: A school using Microsoft 365; a start-up hosting its app on AWS.
items.examTip: Low cost and scalable, but less control over where data is stored.
keyFacts: Pay-as-you-go, so small organisations avoid buying servers and only pay for what they actually use
Scales up or down instantly, so a business can cope with a busy period without buying extra hardware
Provider maintains and secures the hardware, so the organisation needs fewer IT staff of its own
Data sits on shared infrastructure, so the organisation has less control and must trust the provider's security

items.definition: A mix of private and public cloud: sensitive data stays private, other work goes public.
items.examples: A retailer keeps payment data on private cloud and runs its website on public cloud.
items.examTip: "Best of both" in suitability questions: mention flexibility and cost savings.
keyFacts: Sensitive data kept private, so the organisation can meet security and legal (GDPR) requirements
Cheaper public cloud for everything else, so it avoids paying private-cloud costs for non-sensitive work
Can burst to public cloud when demand spikes, so busy periods are handled without buying extra servers
More complex to manage, because staff must run two systems and keep data moving securely between them

items.definition: Rented virtual servers, storage and networking; you manage the OS and software, the provider the hardware.
items.examTip: IaaS = most control, most responsibility.
keyFacts: Full control over the OS and installed software, so it can be set up exactly as the organisation needs
No hardware to buy, so there is no large upfront cost: the organisation pays only for what it uses
Suits custom infrastructure needs, but needs skilled IT staff because the organisation still manages the OS

items.definition: Software delivered over the internet on subscription; the provider manages everything.
items.examTip: SaaS = no installation, access anywhere. Link it to productivity and remote working.
keyFacts: Nothing to install on devices, so it can be rolled out to staff quickly with little IT support
Works on any device with internet, so staff can work from home or on the move
Provider handles updates, so everyone is always on the latest, patched version without IT staff doing it
Monthly or annual subscription, so costs are spread out but keep going for as long as the software is used

items.definition: A ready-made platform for developers to build and deploy apps without managing servers.
items.examTip: PaaS sits between IaaS (most control) and SaaS (least control).
keyFacts: Developers focus on code, not servers, so apps are built faster and with fewer infrastructure skills
Provider handles the OS, patches and scaling, so the organisation needs fewer system administrators
Faster development with built-in tools (databases, testing), so products reach users sooner
Less flexible than IaaS, because developers must work within the tools and settings the provider offers

items.examples: NHS: private. Start-up: public. Large retailer: hybrid.
items.examTip: Match the model to the scenario: sensitive data → private/hybrid; small budget → public.

subtopics.title: Impact and Implications of Cloud Computing

items.term: Impact and Implications of Cloud Computing for Individuals and Organisations
items.definition: Cloud changes how people store data and use software, and how organisations pay for and run IT.
items.examples: Backing up photos to iCloud; a business replacing its servers with AWS.
items.examTip: Discuss both sides. Benefits: cost, scalability, access. Drawbacks: security, internet dependency, lock-in.
keyFacts: Individuals can access files anywhere, and automatic backups mean losing a device does not lose their data
Organisations spend less upfront on hardware, scale as they grow, and always have up-to-date software
Drawbacks: no internet means no access, and data is held by a third party the organisation must trust
Vendor lock-in makes switching provider hard, and data stored abroad may fall under other countries' laws
items.extendedAnswer: Cloud computing offers significant benefits for organisations, including reduced capital expenditure on hardware and the ability to scale resources up or down based on demand. Employees can access data and applications from any location, supporting remote working and improving productivity. However, organisations face risks: if internet connectivity is lost, access to cloud systems is unavailable, causing disruption. Security concerns arise as data is stored on third-party servers, potentially in different countries, raising data protection compliance issues under GDPR. There is also risk of vendor lock-in, where migrating data away from one provider is costly and complex.

items.definition: An encrypted tunnel over the internet that gives secure remote access to an organisation's network.
items.examples: Staff working from home reaching the company intranet.
items.examTip: VPN = encryption + tunnel + remote access.
keyFacts: Encrypts everything sent between the device and the network, so intercepted data cannot be read
Safe to use on public Wi-Fi, because anyone snooping on the hotspot only sees encrypted traffic
Remote staff can reach internal systems, so they can work from home as if they were in the office
Encryption can slow the connection, because every packet has to be encrypted and decrypted

items.definition: Software to view and control another computer's desktop over a network.
items.examples: IT support fixing a PC with TeamViewer; staff using their office PC from home.
items.examTip: Remote desktop = see and control another machine.
keyFacts: Run apps and open files on the remote PC, so IT staff can fix problems without visiting the user
Needs a stable connection, because a slow or dropped link makes the remote desktop lag or disconnect
Security risk if not protected, as an attacker who gets in has full control of that computer
Often used with a VPN, so the remote session is encrypted and not exposed directly to the internet

subtopics.title: Factors Affecting Use and Selection of Online Systems

items.definition: How well an online system protects data and accounts: encryption, access control, legal compliance.
items.examTip: Always link security to how sensitive the data is and to GDPR.
keyFacts: Provider must be GDPR-compliant, because the organisation is still legally responsible for its customers' data
Encrypt data at rest and in transit, so stolen or intercepted data cannot be read
MFA adds a layer, so a stolen password alone is not enough to get into an account
Breaches bring fines and reputational damage, so customers may leave and the organisation loses income

items.definition: The full cost of an online system: subscriptions, data transfer, training and migration.
items.examTip: Compare ongoing subscription costs with one-off capital costs.
keyFacts: Cloud has a low upfront cost but ongoing fees, so it suits organisations without money to buy servers
On-premise has a high upfront cost but lower running costs, so it can work out cheaper over many years
Pay only for what you use, so the organisation does not waste money on spare capacity
Hidden costs (data transfer, support, training) can push the total well above the advertised price

items.definition: How easy the system is for staff and customers to learn and use.
items.examTip: Link ease of use to training needs and productivity.
keyFacts: Complex systems need more training, which costs time and money before staff are productive
Good design reduces errors, so staff waste less time fixing mistakes and data stays accurate
Affects whether staff adopt it: a system people avoid using wastes the money spent on it

items.definition: Whether the system's functions match what the organisation actually needs.
items.examTip: Match features to the scenario: does it do what the business needs?
keyFacts: Must meet user and organisation needs, otherwise staff fall back on old methods and the system is wasted
Extra features add complexity and cost, so paying for functions nobody uses gives poor value

items.definition: The quality and reliability of the internet connection the system depends on.
items.examTip: Cloud is useless without internet: use this as a drawback.
keyFacts: Unreliable connection means downtime and lost work, because a cloud system cannot be reached offline
Video and large files need high bandwidth, so a slow link makes calls drop and uploads crawl
Rural areas may have poor coverage, so staff there cannot rely on online systems

items.definition: The ability to increase or reduce capacity as demand changes, without major cost or disruption.
items.examTip: Scalability is a key cloud benefit in any suitability question.
keyFacts: Scale up at peak times (e.g. Christmas), so the website stays fast when most customers are buying
Scale down afterwards, so the organisation stops paying for capacity it no longer needs
On-premise is slower and costlier to scale, because new servers must be bought, delivered and set up

subtopics.title: Ways of Communicating and Interacting with Online Communities

items.definition: Platforms where users create, share and interact with content, e.g. Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn.
items.examples: A business marketing on Instagram; a school updating parents on X.
items.examTip: Social media = marketing, communication and community building.
keyFacts: Reaches large audiences instantly, so a business can promote products to thousands at low cost
Used for marketing, customer service and brand building, because customers can talk to the business directly
Negative comments spread fast, so one bad experience can damage the brand's reputation publicly
Platforms collect personal data, which raises privacy concerns about how it is used and shared

items.definition: A blog is a regularly updated written site; a vlog is its video version.
items.examples: A tech reviewer's blog; YouTube tutorials.
items.examTip: One-to-many communication for sharing information.
keyFacts: Builds an audience over time, so regular posts create loyal followers who trust the author
Can earn advertising revenue, so a popular blog or vlog can become a source of income
Comments allow interaction, so the author gets feedback and readers feel part of a community
Used for content marketing: useful posts draw in customers who may then buy the product

items.definition: A website that many users can create and edit together, e.g. Wikipedia.
items.examples: Wikipedia; a company's internal knowledge wiki.
items.examTip: Anyone can edit, so accuracy can be a problem.
keyFacts: Built and updated by the community, so information can be added and corrected quickly
Free to access, so anyone can use it to look up information
Edits may be unverified, so information can be wrong or deliberately vandalised and needs checking
Used internally for documentation, so staff share know-how in one place everyone can update

items.definition: Online spaces where several users talk in real time by text; public or private.
items.examTip: Chatrooms are real-time (synchronous); forums are not.
keyFacts: Real-time group conversation, so several people can discuss and get answers immediately
Public or invite-only, so organisations can keep private discussions limited to chosen members
Risks include cyberbullying, grooming and inappropriate content, so chatrooms need moderation

items.definition: Real-time text chat between individuals or small groups, e.g. WhatsApp or Teams.
items.examples: WhatsApp with friends; Teams at work.
items.examTip: Faster and less formal than email.
keyFacts: Quicker than email for short queries, so problems are sorted in seconds rather than hours
Supports files, voice and video, so a quick chat can turn into a call without switching app
Can blur work and personal time, because staff feel they must reply to messages out of hours
Often end-to-end encrypted, so only the sender and recipient can read the messages

items.definition: Audio (sometimes video) episodes published online to listen to on demand.
items.examTip: On-demand, one-way, one-to-many.
keyFacts: Listener chooses when to listen, so people fit episodes around commuting, exercise or chores
Cheap to produce, as it only needs a microphone and editing software, so small creators can start easily
No live interaction, so listeners cannot ask questions or get answers during the episode

items.definition: Discussion boards where users post and reply in threads in their own time.
items.examples: Reddit; Stack Overflow; product support forums.
items.examTip: Forums are asynchronous and searchable; chatrooms are real-time.
keyFacts: Posts stay up and are searchable, so answers to common problems can be found again later
No need to be online together, so people in different time zones can still take part
Quality depends on moderation, because without it threads fill with spam, wrong answers or abuse

items.definition: How easy, fast, available and accessible the platform is to use.
items.examTip: Ask: is it fast, always available, and usable by people with disabilities?
keyFacts: Poor usability drives users away, because people give up on platforms that are confusing to use
Slow performance frustrates users, so they leave and engagement drops
Downtime loses revenue, because users cannot buy, post or communicate while the platform is down
Must work with assistive technology, so disabled users are not excluded (and the law is met)

items.definition: Whether the platform's features match what its users actually need.
items.examTip: Tie the platform choice back to the users in the scenario.
keyFacts: Missing features reduce engagement, because users move to a platform that does what they need
Feedback reveals unmet needs, so the organisation knows which improvements to make first

items.definition: The cost of setting up and running a platform: subscriptions, hosting, moderation, staff.
keyFacts: Free platforms mean less control, because the provider decides the features, rules and adverts
Moderation costs money, because staff or tools are needed to keep content safe
Hidden costs (premium features, advertising) can make a 'free' platform expensive to use properly

items.definition: How well users' personal data is protected and whether it is shared with third parties.
items.examTip: Link privacy to GDPR: data must be handled lawfully.
keyFacts: GDPR requires consent, so platforms must ask before collecting and using personal data
Platforms may sell data to advertisers, so users get targeted adverts and lose control of their data
Users may not know what is collected, so they cannot make an informed choice about using the platform
Needs a clear privacy policy, so users can see what data is held, why, and who it is shared with

items.definition: Protecting accounts and data on the platform from hacking and malicious content.
keyFacts: Strong passwords and MFA, so accounts are much harder to take over even if a password leaks
Malicious links spread through communities, because users trust messages that seem to come from friends
HTTPS encrypts data in transit, so logins and messages cannot be read if intercepted

items.definition: Time when the platform is unavailable, so users cannot access or communicate.
keyFacts: Planned maintenance can be scheduled for quiet times and announced, unlike unexpected outages
Critical systems need high uptime (99.9%), because even short outages stop essential services
Loses revenue and trust, because users cannot buy or communicate and may move to a rival

items.definition: The training staff and users need to use and manage the platform well.
keyFacts: Staff need training to moderate, so they know how to deal with abuse and harmful posts correctly
Costs time and money, because staff are away from their normal work while they learn
Needed again when the platform updates, because new features and layouts change how it works

items.definition: How easily the platform connects to systems the organisation already uses.
keyFacts: Should link to email, CRM and analytics, so customer data flows between systems automatically
Poor integration means duplicate work, because staff re-type the same data into several systems
APIs make integration possible, by letting different systems send data to each other directly

items.definition: The effect of the platform on how much staff get done.
keyFacts: Speeds up collaboration and problem-solving, because staff can share files and get answers quickly
Constant notifications and social media distract, so staff lose focus and get less done
AUPs help manage use, by setting clear rules on when and how platforms should be used at work

items.definition: The rules organisations set for how staff behave on online communities, e.g. an AUP.
items.examTip: Link to AUPs (F1.1.6): rules protect reputation and keep the organisation within the law.
keyFacts: AUPs set what is and isn't allowed, so staff know the rules and can be disciplined if they break them
Staff represent the company online, so a careless post can damage the organisation's reputation
Policies must follow GDPR and employment law, otherwise the organisation can face fines or claims
